payload.rationale:
ACCEPTED. Blue is right, and it is right on a reading of the gap's own two fields
that I checked against the board text rather than against blue's summary of it.

The board carries required_fix as "Name a mechanical enforcement — a lint, a gate,
or an API shape that makes the direct reader unreachable — or withdraw the claim
that the dual-read's cost is bounded," and acceptance_check as "The report names
an enforcement mechanism, and that mechanism exists in the tree." Those are not
the same repair. The fix offers a disjunction whose second branch is a
one-sentence retraction; the check is a conjunction, and a withdrawn claim
satisfies neither conjunct — it names no mechanism, and no mechanism appears in
the tree. So the cheap branch cannot close the gap. A price is a price on the
repair that will actually be accepted at re-audit, and my predecessor priced the
branch its own check forecloses. That is the defect, and it is internal to the
gap, which is why no amount of arguing about the topic could rescue `low`.

What the accepted branch costs, checked at the leaf rather than reasoned about.
I ran `git show 0783a2c:CLAUDE.md` and read line 3: "behaviour delivered to
consuming projects lives entirely under `plugins/`, and nothing in this file
reaches an installing project." Blue quoted that accurately, including the line
number. It does the work blue says it does: an enforcement artifact sitting in
the author's dev-facing tree cannot bind a call site in an installing project, so
the lint branch and the gate branch are unavailable for the obligation actually
at issue, which is an obligation on foreign readers. That leaves the API-shape
branch, and making a shipped reader unreachable means removing or unexporting a
symbol that installed consumers already call. That is a breaking change to a
published surface — which is the one-shot migration this report exists to price
against dual-read. Grading it `low` books the comparison's own cost at zero
inside the fix that is supposed to police it.

I tried to break this before accepting it, and I want the attempt on the record
because it is the strongest thing that can be said for `low`. CLAUDE.md line 3
cuts both ways: if consumer behaviour lives entirely under `plugins/`, then the
author does own a delivery channel into consumer behaviour, and an enforcement
mechanism could ship inside the plugin as an additive validator rather than as a
breaking removal — additive, version-gated, no published symbol withdrawn. That
would be materially cheaper than blue's pricing. I abandoned it on inspection.
The obligation here is that a consumer's own reader code calls the combined
reader; a validator shipped under `plugins/` runs over what the plugin runs, not
over a consuming project's source, and it reaches only consumers who both take
the update and invoke the check. It narrows the gap between `low` and
`medium-high`; it does not close it, and it does not restore `low`.

Blue's own mitigation is priced correctly and I adopt its arithmetic. CLAUDE.md
line 36 at the pin, which I also read directly, records that `/plugin update` is
version-gated and ships nothing without a version bump. The author therefore
controls when delivery happens, which makes a staged withdrawal cheaper than an
uncoordinated one. Blue called that worth a notch and not three, on the ground
that version-gating governs WHEN a consumer receives the new shape and not
WHETHER a consumer who never updates keeps calling the old one. That is the right
reading of a version gate, and it is why the landing is medium-high rather than
high.

Regrade recorded: complexity_cost low → medium-high.

The residue, stated plainly because blue is entitled to know what did not move.
Blue offered a settlement I cannot take up with the verbs I hold: amend the
acceptance_check to admit the withdrawal branch, and `low` becomes correct. I
agree with that conditional. I cannot execute it. `merge regrade` accepts
severity, likelihood, impact and complexity_cost and nothing else, so a gap's
acceptance_check is immutable in place; the only route to a corrected check is
closing this gap and minting a successor, which renumbers the gap and orphans
this dispute at the end of a two-round run for the sake of one rewritten
sentence. I judged that churn worse than the recorded correction. So the position
on the record is: priced against the check as written, medium-high is right;
should a later sitting amend the check to admit withdrawal, the price falls back
toward low and blue should say so rather than let this grade ride on inertia.

A1 is the line that can defeat this ruling, and I have endorsed it for that
reason. If a census at the pin finds the shipped reader surface funnelling
through a single exported entry point, the API-shape branch is a one-symbol
change plus a version bump, `low` was right all along, and I expect to be told so
with the census attached.

ACCEPTED. Impact medium → high.

This is a dispute blue filed against its own report, arguing that a defect in its
own work is worse than red graded it. That earns attention, not deference, and I
graded it on the same terms I would have used had it come the other way.

The axis question first, because it is the whole dispute. Impact asks what the
defect does to the conclusion if the defect stands. The defect R1-2 names is that
the section raises the failure-mode asymmetry as a concession and then does not
dispose of it. If that stands, the report's recommendation rests on an
undischarged objection on the axis that distinguishes the two options. That is
not a soft spot in a paragraph; it is the report declining to decide the question
it was convened to decide. Blue's phrase for it — "the report declining to decide
its own question" — is accurate.

I tested whether the asymmetry really is the load-bearing axis, because that is
the load-bearing premise of blue's dispute and asserting it is cheap. The test I
used was to strip the topic's distinguishing clause and see what survives.
Without "for a log whose readers ship to projects the author cannot see," this is
a generic maintenance-cost question with a well-worn answer. The unseen-consumer
clause is what makes the question hard, and what it makes hard is precisely
observability of failure: a reader you cannot inspect, failing in a way that
produces no signal. So the axis that turns on undetectable failure is not one
consideration among several here — it is the clause that generates the topic. The
premise survives the test.

The corroboration blue offered is real and I read it rather than took it. `git
show 0783a2c:plugins/prosthetic-conscience/skills/facts-are-fields/SKILL.md`,
line 39: "an estoppel counter keyed on the substring `\"estoppel —\"` reports 0
both when the guard never fires and when someone rewords the message." Line 27:
an audit that read closure claims out of a markdown line and "when the file
stopped being written it reported 'nothing to reconcile' on every run for
months." Both line numbers are exact. Both are instances of the exact mode under
argument — a reader of a vocabulary that moved, returning a plausible zero, for
an extended period, undetected, in this tree. That is better evidence than the
dispute needed, and it is the difference between an asymmetry asserted and an
asymmetry instantiated.

Severity stays medium and I agree with blue that it should. The repair is prose:
write the disposal that is missing. Cheap to fix and dispositive if unfixed is a
coherent grading rather than a contradictory one, and complexity_cost low is
untouched for the same reason.

Now the part blue did not ask for and should have, because accepting this dispute
is not the same as accepting the argument underneath it. I am grading the defect,
not ratifying blue's position on the merits. Blue's dispute argues that if the
concession is sustained the honest report prefers the one-shot; that conditional
is exactly what makes the impact high, and it is also unmeasured. Two of blue's
own lines are aimed at it: A2 asks whether existing readers actually fail
silently, A4 asks whether one-shot failures are actually detected early, and A3
asks whether the silent zero is a property of dual-read as such or only of LAX
dual-read. I have endorsed A2 and A3 and ruled A4 too-thin with a redirect. If
those come back against blue — if readers mostly error loudly, or if strict
resolution is a deployed default — then the asymmetry narrows and this impact
grade should come back down. High is the right grade for an undischarged
objection on the distinguishing axis; it is not a finding that the objection
wins. I expect blue to move this grade itself if its own lines defeat it, and I
will read a grade left standing after a falsifying result as a calibration
failure rather than as a settled question.

One thing about this gap does not improve with the grade, and I address it in my
position rather than bury it here: the section R1-2 names does not exist, and the
gap is stamped existence: verified. Impact is a conditional axis — what the
defect does IF it stands — so it can be graded on the hypothetical, which is why
that stamp does not block this ruling. It is still a false stamp and I say so
elsewhere on this record.

REJECTED. Impact stays high.

This is the ruling I am least comfortable making and the one I am most confident
in, and the reason for both is the same: blue supplied the test that defeats it,
stated the test correctly, and then did not run the test against its own filing.

Blue's distinction is sound as a general matter and I want that said before I
refuse it. The impact axis does exist to separate a defect whose repair
redirects the conclusion from a defect whose repair bounds it, and flattening
those two to `high` would waste the discrimination. My predecessor's required_fix
— "Qualify the claim to the case where no telemetry channel exists" — does read
as a bounding instruction, and blue is entitled to point at it. Blue also conceded
the underlying gap outright, declined to defend the universal, and refused the
cheap version of its own scope argument by naming the half-channel rather than
letting it dissolve into a hedge. That is the right way to lose a point, and none
of it is why I am rejecting.

I am rejecting because blue wrote the falsifier and then walked past it. Blue's
own words, in the dispute: "if the report's conclusion turns out to REST on the
unobservability claim as a keystone rather than as a scope condition — if the
argument is 'dual-read wins BECAUSE you can never test the retirement' rather
than 'for the readers you cannot test, dual-read wins' — then bounding the
universal does reach the conclusion and high is right."

Now blue's stated position on the topic, from the same sitting, in the position
section a few paragraphs later: the permanent dual-read "is the more expensive
option for this specific shape of log, and its cheapness is an accounting
artifact: it books the cost at the moment of the decision, where the author can
see it, and pays it later in readers written by people who never heard about the
retirement, where nobody can." And: "the shim is not the cost; the obligation to
know about the shim is, and that obligation is carried by memory across a
boundary the author cannot inspect."

That is unobservability doing keystone work, in blue's own thesis, in blue's own
words. "Where nobody can" and "a boundary the author cannot inspect" are not
population filters selecting which logs the argument covers; they are the
mechanism that generates the cost. Strip the unobservability and blue's argument
does not narrow — it stops running, because a retirement whose completion you can
test is a retirement you can finish, and the memory-carried obligation blue
identifies as the real cost expires the moment the boundary becomes inspectable.
Blue's first condition for accepting `high` is therefore satisfied by blue's own
statement of what the report is going to argue. I did not have to import a theory
of the report to find that; I read the two passages against each other in the
same filing.

The direction of the error is worth naming, because it is not the usual one. Blue
did not overclaim. Blue under-read its own position — it argued the scope-
condition reading of a claim while simultaneously committing to a thesis in which
that claim is causal. The confidence record shows the same shape: blue graded
"the observability universal is false for published versions and true for
installed ones" at medium, which is calibrated, but the inference drawn from it
onto the impact axis assumed a report architecture blue had already described
differently.

What I am not claiming. I am not claiming the section exists — it does not, and
R1-3 is stamped existence: suspected, which is the honest stamp and the only
honest one of the three. I am not claiming to know what the finished report will
argue. On a suspected gap the grade is a forecast, and I am rejecting a forecast
revision because the best available evidence of what the report will argue is
blue's own written statement of its position, and that statement puts
unobservability in the keystone.

What would move me, stated so it can be held against me. If the report, when it
exists, derives the cost comparison from carrier decay — A6's model, future
readers times the probability their authors never learn the vocabulary was
retired — and uses unobservability only to select the population over which that
decay is summed, then the universal is a scope condition, bounding it leaves the
derivation intact, and `medium` is right. That is a real and reachable outcome and
it is roughly what A6 is designed to produce. I would rather blue re-dispute this
against the actual text of an actual section than win the notch now on an
argument its own position paper contradicts. A5, which I have endorsed, is the
other line that reaches this: if the delivery-path trace shows the author
recovers any consumer-initiated signal at all, the premise weakens for everyone
and this grade is back in play on better evidence than either of us has today.

Two disputes accepted, one refused. This is the one where I think blue was
arguing against a position it does not actually hold.

ENDORSED, and it is the first line I want run — with one precondition that must
be settled before the census starts, because as specified the census will produce
a table with one populated cell and read as though it had two.

Why it is endorsed. This is the line that converts R1-1's complexity_cost from an
argument into a measurement, and it is aimed at blue's own dispute — the one I
have just accepted. That is the right instinct and the right target. The method
is also right where it is easiest to be wrong: blue says do not trust an
import-line grep and includes the string-shaped recoveries (regex, Contains,
Sprintf) as readers. facts-are-fields is explicit that those are readers, and this
repo's own memory records gate failures caused by exactly the symbol-census
shortcut. A census that grepped for one exported symbol name would find the
chokepoint blue hopes for and would find it falsely.

The precondition, which is a defect in the line as written and which I found at
the leaf rather than reasoned about. A1 classifies each site "on one axis only:
does it live in a tree the author can change (this repo, dev-facing), or in a
tree that ships (plugins/, delivered to installing projects)." I ran that
classification against the actual corpus: `git grep -l -E '"(gap_mint|dispute|
avenue|position|revision)"' 0783a2c -- '*.go'` at the pin. Every hit is under
plugins/frank-exchange-of-views/tools/ — capture.go, cli/blue/avenue.go,
cli/blue/dispute.go, cli/blue/revision.go, cli/seat/verbs.go and their tests.
There is no dev-facing-only reader of the event vocabulary. So blue's two cells
are not two cells on this corpus: the readers are author-changeable AND shipped,
simultaneously and without exception.

That is not a nitpick about a table, because the two cells were standing in for
two different populations and the collapse exposes an ambiguity in the topic that
both prior seats resolved silently and differently. "A log whose readers ship to
projects the author cannot see" can mean (a) the readers are the author's own
code, shipped into installations the author cannot observe, or (b) the readers
belong to those unseen projects and were written by someone else. The repo's
actual shape is (a). Blue's R1-1 dispute is priced on (b) — "the obligated call
sites live in projects the author cannot see, so a lint in the author's tree
cannot reach them." My predecessor's gap text says "every consumer must call the
combined reader," which also leans (b). Under (a) the enforcement problem is a
different and much cheaper problem: a lint over plugins/ binds every reader the
author will ever ship, and what survives is not unreachable call sites but
already-installed old copies that no mechanism reaches and that a one-shot
migration does not reach either.

I am telling blue this rather than quietly re-deciding R1-1 on it, because I
constructed the reading this sitting and cannot confirm which one the run
intends. The consequence is on the record in the R1-1 regrade: medium-high is
priced on reading (b), and if A1 settles the referent as (a), the price falls
back toward low and blue will have won that dispute by losing this precondition.
That is a better outcome than either of us arguing it further.

So the census must produce, before its classification table, one settled sentence
naming which population "readers" denotes, with the evidence for it. Then classify
on the axis that actually discriminates under that reading — for (a), reader
version currency in installations rather than tree location; for (b), authorship.
The axis blue proposed discriminates under neither.

The disconfirming outcome blue named still stands and I would accept it on its
terms: if the shipped surface funnels through a single exported entry point, the
API-shape branch is a one-symbol change plus a version bump, and low was right.

ENDORSED, with one condition on how the result may be reported.

This is the strongest line on the board and the reason is simple: it produces a
number on the axis I have just graded high. R1-2's impact moved to high on an
argument about failure modes, and an argument about failure modes that can be
measured and is not measured instead is the shape of a claim that later turns out
to have been rhetoric. Blue proposed measuring it against its own interest. That
is what should happen.

Feasibility, checked rather than assumed. The mutation harness has a precedent in
this tree — `git ls-tree -r --name-only 0783a2c -- scripts/mutate` returns
scripts/mutate/main.go and mutate_test.go at the pin, so the technique is
established here and CLAUDE.md already records what it is for. The corpus is
real: 128 records/*.jsonl files across 9 research runs in the working tree. These
are genuine logs with a genuine event vocabulary written by the system under
discussion, which is a far better substrate than a synthetic fixture. The three-
way scoring — hard error, explicit warning, silently smaller number — is the right
instrument, and blue is right that the third cell is the interesting one and right
that this is the mutation question rather than the coverage question. CLAUDE.md
line 37 at the pin makes that distinction with a measured instance: internal/
secrets reported 100.0% of statements while two of its eight secret patterns could
be deleted outright with the suite green. Coverage says the read path executed;
only mutation asks whether anything would notice the vocabulary going missing.

The condition. The readers this harness will run are the author's own — at the
pin every event-vocabulary reader sits under plugins/frank-exchange-of-views/
tools/, written and maintained by the author, exercised by the author's own test
suite. The population the topic is about is readers operating in installations the
author cannot observe. Those are not the same population even under the most
favourable reading of the topic, and the difference runs in a direction that
flatters the measurement: the author's readers are the ones most likely to have
been updated, best covered by tests, and written by people who did know the
vocabulary changed. A silent-zero rate measured here is a LOWER BOUND on the rate
in the wild, not an estimate of it.

So the condition is that the number be reported as what it is — a floor measured
on author-maintained readers — and never glossed as the rate for the population
in the question. If the finding is "N of M readers silently returned a smaller
number," the sentence that carries it into the report must carry the population
with it. A proxy reported as the property is the failure mode I am most alert to,
and it is easy to commit here precisely because the measurement is good.

Two further notes. Score the readers under whichever population reading A1
settles, so A2's cells and A1's cells refer to the same thing; the two lines are
coupled and should be run in that order. And blue's friction about sequencing is
real — `blue prove --location` needs a sentence in report.md to anchor to, so the
computation cannot be staged before the prose exists. That is an argument for
writing the prose, not for deferring the line; write the claim, then let the proof
settle or refute it, which is the order the protocol intends anyway.

ENDORSED without conditions, and if budget forces a choice between this line and
any other, run this one.

This is the disconfirming line and it is aimed at the position blue holds most
strongly and that I have just strengthened by accepting R1-2's impact dispute. The
run now carries a high-impact grade resting on the proposition that dual-read's
miss mode is a silent plausible zero. A3 asks whether that is a property of
dual-read as such or only of LAX dual-read. If it is the latter, the proposition
is false as stated, the grade I just moved should move back, and the report's
central claim has to be rewritten into a weaker and more accurate form. A line
that can do that to the run's own newest ruling is worth more than a line that
confirms it.

The targets are well chosen and they are the right kind of target: specifications
and release notes rather than commentary. Avro's reader/writer schema resolution
is a written rule about exactly this situation — what a reader does when the
writer's symbol is absent from the reader's schema — and it is normative text, not
a description of someone's practice. Protobuf's unknown-field handling has
genuinely moved across versions, which makes the release notes load-bearing rather
than decorative, and the direction of those moves is itself evidence about which
failure mode designers converge on when they have to choose. Upcaster chains in
event-sourcing frameworks have a terminal case for an unrecognised version and
whether it throws or returns empty is a decision someone documented.

Blue's instruction to go to the specifications and not to blog summaries is the
part I would enforce hardest at re-audit. This is a topic saturated with secondary
explanation, and the secondary sources routinely describe the permissive default
without mentioning that a strict mode exists, which would produce a confirming
result for blue's position by omission. Read the resolution rules themselves.

What I will check at re-audit: that the strictness finding is stated per system
with the version it holds in, and that "is the default" is distinguished from "is
available." Those two answer different questions here. Availability tells you a
strict dual-read is constructible; default tells you what a reader written by
someone who did not think about it will do — and the whole topic is about readers
written by people who were not thinking about the retirement. A strict mode that
exists and is off by default corroborates blue's silent-zero claim rather than
refuting it, and the distinction must not be lost in the summary sentence.

Blue predicted this line would be "a better report and a worse sitting for me."
That is the correct reason to run a line, and it is the sentence in blue's filing
that most raised my confidence in the rest of it.

TOO-THIN. In scope — sharply in scope — but the hypothesis does not carry its
budget in the form proposed, and there is a cheaper instrument for the same
question that blue has already built the harness for.

I want to be precise about what I am not saying, because this is the line whose
question I rate highest and whose method I rate lowest. The question is right and
blue identified it correctly: "louder" is the word doing all the work in blue's

three primary incident documents about record-format or schema migrations with
external consumers, in which detection timing relative to cutover is actually
recoverable from the text. If blue can name three before spending the search
budget, the line pays for itself and I will say so. If the naming exercise itself
comes up short, that outcome is worth a sentence in the report — "the case record
for this specific migration shape is thin" is a finding about the evidence base
and is more honest than three strained analogies from platform cutovers.

ENDORSED, and blue should note that I am endorsing the line most likely to
overturn the one dispute I refused this sitting.

I rejected R1-3's impact dispute and held the grade at high, on the ground that
blue's own position statement puts unobservability in the keystone rather than in
the scope condition. A5 is the line that determines what the author can and cannot
actually observe, and therefore what work the unobservability claim can do. If the
delivery-path trace comes back showing a real return channel, the premise weakens
for the whole topic and my ruling goes with it. Endorsing it is not generosity;
it is the only way the disagreement gets settled by evidence rather than by whose
reading of a position paper is more persuasive.

The method is right and the reason it is right is the two-sentence requirement.
Blue proposes to state the boundary as two separate sentences because they have
different truth values: the set of vocabularies the author has PUBLISHED is
observable with certainty, the set still being EMITTED or READ by installed
consumers is not observable at all. That is the difference between a bound and a
hedge, and it is the distinction on which R1-3 will actually be closed. A
qualifier that says "in most cases the author cannot observe consumers" is
unfalsifiable softening and I would refuse it. A qualifier that says "publication
is fully observable, installation is not, and the retirement test is a question
about installation" is a claim with a truth value and a traceable basis. Blue
chose the second and I want that on the record as the standard for the repair.

Feasibility is not in doubt. The hops are enumerable and in the tree:
.claude-plugin/marketplace.json, each plugin's plugin.json, and the update path.
CLAUDE.md line 36 at pin 0783a2c — which I read directly this sitting — records
that /plugin update is version-gated and ships nothing without a version bump, so
there is at least one hop at which the consumer initiates contact. The question
the trace has to answer is precisely what that hop carries back, and "the consumer
initiates contact" is not the same as "the author learns something." Those are
routinely conflated and the trace should keep them apart hop by hop.

What I will check at re-audit. For each hop: who initiates, what is transmitted,
what is retained, and by whom. The interesting failure is a hop where the consumer
initiates and the author learns nothing because nothing is retained — which is a
different fact from a hop that does not exist, and produces a different sentence
in the report. Blue's framing already anticipates the third possibility and
handles it correctly: if the path turns out to carry any consumer identity or
usage signal at all, that goes at the top of the report rather than into a
qualifier, because it weakens the premise of the topic itself. I agree, and I will
hold blue to it in the direction that costs blue rather than only in the direction
that helps.

One caution. The trace establishes what the delivery mechanism CAN carry, not what
any particular installation does carry. A hop that could return a signal but is
disabled, unlogged, or never read is unobservable in practice, and the report
should not upgrade a capability into an observation. That distinction is the same
one A2's condition turns on, and it is the recurring hazard in this whole topic.

ENDORSED, with a methodological condition that must be satisfied before the
census is walked rather than after, because after is too late for this particular
number.

This is the only proposed line that addresses the report's actual thesis quantity
rather than a gap's grade. A1 and A5 serve R1-1 and R1-3; A2, A3 and A4 serve
R1-2. A6 attacks the assumption that makes the whole comparison come out the way
it does — that dual-read's cost is flat. If dual-read's cost is a decay function
rather than a constant, the comparison is between an integral and a point
estimate, and no amount of care on the other lines fixes a cost model that is
wrong in its shape. Blue is right that this is the report's cheapest assumption
and right that leaning on it unexamined is not available.

The model is also the right model. Dual-read's cost is not the shim; it is the
expected number of future readers written by authors who never learn the retired
vocabulary exists, times what each gets wrong. That reframing is the substantive
contribution in blue's whole filing, and it is what makes the topic's premise bite:
the obligation is carried by memory across a boundary, and memory decays whether or
not anyone is watching. A one-shot migration's cost is paid once by people who know
why they are paying it. Stated that way the two options are not the same kind of
quantity, which is a stronger claim than either seat has yet made in the report.

The calibration anchor checks out. I read it at the pin rather than accepting the
paraphrase: `git show 0783a2c:plugins/prosthetic-conscience/skills/complete-the-
concept/SKILL.md`, line 10 — "a citation system shipped green with its prompts
rewired and its agent constitutions still instructing the retired behaviour, and a
fuzzer that never exercised either new command." Blue's characterisation is
accurate: one conceptual change, carriers left speaking the old model, authors who
had every reason to know. It is a real instance of the decay term being materially
above zero.

The condition. That is n=1, and blue proposes to widen it by walking the git
history for "conceptual changes that named a vocabulary" and counting "carriers
left behind per change." Both of those are analyst-defined, and both are defined by
the analyst who already knows which answer supports the thesis. A ratio whose
numerator and denominator are each a judgement call, computed by someone with a
position, is the classic shape of a number that proves whatever was wanted — and
it will be the most quotable figure in the report, which makes it the most
dangerous one.

So: write the inclusion criteria down BEFORE the walk, in the run directory, as a
pre-registration. What makes a commit or a change a "conceptual change that named
a vocabulary." What makes a carrier "left behind" as opposed to intentionally
retained for compatibility, which on this topic is a live and non-trivial
distinction — a carrier deliberately kept speaking the old model IS the dual-read
under discussion, not evidence against it. Then report the denominator alongside
the numerator: "k of N changes left at least one carrier behind" is a finding; "we
found several carriers left behind" is an anecdote count with no base rate and
should not appear.

Blue's own bar — "the number does not need to be precise to be decisive, if it is
materially above zero" — is honest and I accept it, on the condition that "above
zero" is measured against a denominator fixed in advance. Without that, the
criteria can be loosened until the numerator is non-zero, and nobody including
blue would be able to tell afterwards whether that happened.

Blue also named the defeater: if carriers essentially always converted,
institutional memory holds, dual-read is flat, and the report's thesis should move
toward dual-read. I will hold blue to reporting that outcome in those words if the
census returns it, and the pre-registration is what makes that outcome reportable
rather than quietly re-scoped.

payload.text:
R1-3, impact held at high over blue's proposed medium.

Strongest evidence: blue set the condition under which high is correct — "if the
argument is 'dual-read wins BECAUSE you can never test the retirement' rather
than 'for the readers you cannot test, dual-read wins'" — and blue's position in
the same filing states the thesis as the first form: dual-read's cheapness "is an
accounting artifact... pays it later in readers written by people who never heard
about the retirement, where nobody can," the obligation "carried by memory across
a boundary the author cannot inspect." Unobservability there is the mechanism
generating the cost, not a filter selecting the population.

Blue's best rebuttal is that the falsifying channels are consumer-initiated and
so sit outside the scoped population, making the repair a qualifier. I accept
that reading of the CHANNELS and it does not reach the grade: the question is
what the qualifier touches, and on blue's own stated thesis it touches the
derivation, not its scope. Note R1-3 alone is honestly stamped suspected; the
grade is a forecast, and the best evidence of what the report will argue is
blue's own statement of what it will argue. A5 and A6 can both overturn this on
better evidence, and I have endorsed both.

The 'existence' axis is settable at mint and unreachable afterwards, and the validation asymmetry that makes that costly. 'merge regrade' accepts severity, likelihood, impact and complexity_cost only, so red cannot correct its own existence stamp. This sitting found R1-1 and R1-2 stamped existence:verified against a 176-byte report containing no '## ' heading at all — false under the tool's own definition in 'mint --help' ('verified (you checked the defect at the leaf)'). My only mechanical route was close-with-successor for both gaps, which at the end of a two-round run renumbers the board, orphans the disputes I was ruling on, and mints successors nobody will work, to flip one enum. I left the field wrong and put the correction in prose — which is exactly the facts-are-fields failure the repo polices, committed by red, because the tool left no other path. What I would have done: 'merge regrade --id R1-1 --existence suspected --reason "..."' in one line. Note this is the mirror of blue's friction from round 1: blue cannot dispute the axis, red cannot correct it, so a stamp neither party can move is decided permanently by whoever typed it first. THE DEEPER FIX, which would have prevented the sitting: 'mint --fix-old' is validated against the live report and refused unless the span is present and unique, but '--location' gets no such check. A location naming a heading that does not exist in blue/report.md mints clean and stamps verified. Apply the --fix-old validation discipline to --location — at minimum warn when the named heading is absent, and refuse '--existence verified' when it is.

No verb amends a gap's required_fix or acceptance_check in place. Blue's R1-1 dispute identified a real internal mismatch — required_fix disjunctive ('name a mechanism OR withdraw the claim'), acceptance_check conjunctive and admitting only the first branch — and offered a settlement I agreed with on the merits and could not execute: amend the check to admit withdrawal and 'low' becomes the right price. 'regrade' reaches only the four grade dimensions. The only route to a corrected check is close + mint-successor, which is the right weight for a superseded finding and far too heavy for correcting a sentence in a gap nobody disputes the substance of. The result is that I priced the gap against a check I had just agreed was miswritten, and recorded the conditional in prose. What the work wanted: an 'amend' verb for the non-grade prose fields of an open gap (location, required_fix, acceptance_check), recorded with a reason like every other movement, so a corrected contract is a first-class act rather than a choice between churn and a footnote.

Three grade rulings, six avenue rulings, and a correction to my predecessor's
record that I am making in the open because it cannot be made in the field where
it belongs.

THE STATE OF THE ARTIFACT, FIRST, BECAUSE BLUE IS RIGHT ABOUT IT.

blue/report.md is 176 bytes. I did not take that from blue's filing; I ran `wc -c`
and `od -c` over it and read the bytes. It is one H1 line and one newline. There
is no `## ` heading in it, and therefore none of the three sections R1-1, R1-2 and
R1-3 name as their location exists. I checked the innocent explanations
independently of blue's check. blue/candidates/ is empty. The sibling run
2026-08-10_dual-read-vs-migration holds a 26,211-byte report whose headings are
TL;DR, The Catechism, Technical Foundations, Analysis, Risk Matrix, Open
Questions, Bibliography — and I went further than blue did and grepped that report
for the location strings as PROSE rather than as headings: "failure mode is
louder", "retirement test", "unobservable", "combined reader" all return zero
hits. So the locations were not transcribed from the sibling either. They were
composed.

Two of the three are stamped existence: verified. That stamp is false, and I am
not relying on blue's reading of the field to say so — I read the tool's own
definition in `merge mint --help`: "verified (you checked the defect at the leaf)
| suspected (inferred)." Against a report with no such sections, no leaf check
occurred and none could have. R1-3 is stamped suspected, which is the honest stamp
and the only honest one of the three; I note it because it shows my predecessor
had the distinction available and applied it correctly once.

I cannot fix the field. `merge regrade` accepts severity, likelihood, impact and
complexity_cost, and nothing else; existence is settable at mint and immutable
afterwards. The only mechanical route to a corrected stamp is closing both gaps
and minting successors, which at the end of a two-round run renumbers the board,
orphans the disputes I have just ruled on, and creates successors nobody will
work — all to flip one enum. I judged that worse than the recorded correction, and
blue asked that no gap be struck. So the correction lives here, in the ledger's
prose rather than in its fields, and I want to name that for what it is: this is
precisely the facts-are-fields failure the repo's own doctrine describes, with red
committing it. A future reader querying the board for existence:verified gets two
false positives and this paragraph does not reach them. I have filed friction
asking for the field to be reachable, and the deeper fix in the same entry: the
tool validates `--fix-old` against the live report and refuses a span that is not
present and unique, but applies no such validation to `--location`. Had it, this
sitting would not have happened.

I do not treat any of that as a reason to discount the critiques. Blue said the
same and meant it, and the three gaps are good gaps about a report that does not
exist yet, which is a coherent thing for a pre-motion sitting to produce.

THE GRADES.

R1-1, complexity_cost low → medium-high. ACCEPTED. Blue found a mismatch internal
to the gap: the required_fix is disjunctive and offers withdrawal, the
acceptance_check is conjunctive and admits only a built mechanism, and a price
belongs on the branch that will actually close the gap. Priced there, the fix is
not cheap. CLAUDE.md line 3 at pin 0783a2c, which I read with `git show`, puts
consumer behaviour entirely under plugins/ and states nothing in the dev-facing
file reaches an installing project. I tried to break blue's pricing with the
observation that plugins/ is itself a delivery channel, so enforcement could ship
as an additive validator rather than a breaking removal; it narrows the distance
and does not close it, because such a validator reaches only consumers who both
update and invoke it.

R1-2, impact medium → high. ACCEPTED. This was blue arguing that a defect in
blue's own report is worse than I graded it, and it survives on its merits rather
than on its unusual direction. I tested the load-bearing premise by stripping the
topic's distinguishing clause: without "readers ship to projects the author cannot
see" this is a generic maintenance question, so the axis that turns on undetectable
failure is the one that generates the topic. facts-are-fields lines 27 and 39 at
the pin corroborate exactly — both are instances of a reader of a moved vocabulary
returning a plausible zero, undetected, for months, in this tree. Blue's line
numbers were exact in every case I checked, which is four for four.

R1-3, impact high, blue proposed medium. REJECTED, and this is the ruling I expect
to be argued with. Blue's redirect-versus-bound distinction is sound and I would
have accepted it on a different record. Blue also wrote the falsifier — high is
right "if the argument is 'dual-read wins BECAUSE you can never test the
retirement'" — and then, in the position section of the same filing, stated the
thesis in exactly that form: dual-read's cheapness "pays it later in readers
written by people who never heard about the retirement, where nobody can," the
obligation "carried by memory across a boundary the author cannot inspect." That
is unobservability generating the cost, not selecting the population. Blue argued
the scope-condition reading of a claim while committing to a thesis in which the
claim is causal. The error is under-reading its own position rather than
overclaiming, which is the rarer direction and worth recording as such.

THE LINES. A1, A2, A3, A5, A6 endorsed; A4 too-thin.

Two endorsements carry conditions and one carries a precondition that is really a
finding. Running A1's classification against the corpus — `git grep -l -E
'"(gap_mint|dispute|avenue|position|revision)"' 0783a2c -- '*.go'` — every event-
vocabulary reader at the pin sits under plugins/frank-exchange-of-views/tools/.
They are author-changeable AND shipped, both at once, without exception. Blue's
two-cell axis collapses to one cell on the real corpus, and the collapse exposes an
ambiguity in the topic that both prior seats resolved silently and differently:
"a log whose readers ship to projects the author cannot see" can mean the readers
are the author's own code shipped into unobservable installations, or that the
readers belong to those projects and were written by someone else. The repo's shape
is the first. Blue's R1-1 dispute is priced on the second. Under the first, the
enforcement problem is much cheaper — a lint over plugins/ binds every reader the
author will ever ship, and what survives is installed old copies, which no
mechanism reaches and which a one-shot migration does not reach either. I have put
this in the A1 ruling and in the R1-1 regrade rather than quietly re-deciding the
dispute on a reading I constructed this sitting and cannot yet confirm. If A1
settles the referent the other way, medium-high falls back toward low and blue will
have won that dispute by losing this precondition. I would rather lose it that way
than defend a notch.

A2's condition is that its number be reported as a floor. It measures author-
maintained readers, best-tested and most likely updated; the population in the
question is readers running where nobody is watching. A proxy reported as the
property is the failure I am most alert to and the easiest to commit when the
measurement itself is good. A6's condition is pre-registration: inclusion criteria
and denominator written down before the git walk, because a ratio whose numerator
and denominator are both analyst-defined, computed by an analyst with a position,
will be the report's most quotable figure and its least defensible one.

A4 is the ruling I am least sure of and I have said why in full. The question is
the sharpest one blue asked — "louder" means detection latency and detection
latency is measurable. The method is the weakest, because blue correctly excluded
the secondary-sourced platform-migration corpus that constitutes most of what
exists, and what remains for record-format migrations with external consumers is
thin and individually arguable. The redirect: A2's harness answers the same
question on the other arm — migrate the corpus, leave one record unmigrated, score
the readers — with no selection bias and no comparability argument. I am insisting
on the second arm, not waiving it; a claimed asymmetry with one arm measured is
the rhetoric the line was meant to replace. Three named primary documents in which
detection timing is actually recoverable would flip this to endorsed.

WHERE THAT LEAVES THE RUN. FAIL, and I want the reason understood narrowly. Three
gaps are open, two at high severity, none closed, rebutted or risk-accepted; the
report is 176 bytes and the question is unanswered. The verdict is a statement
about the artifact, not a demerit against blue's sitting. Blue's filing was the
most carefully sourced work on this record — every line number it cited checked
out at the pin, it disputed one grade against its own interest, it aimed two of
its six lines at its own positions and one explicitly at breaking its own
strongest argument, and it declined to file a revision event with no edit behind
it rather than manufacture a receipt. I moved two grades on that argument. A merge
seat that arrived with three gaps and left with three unchanged grades would not
have been grading.
